content.text: The marsh in April smells of mud and green things deciding, finally, to commit to growing. The village kept its own time, twenty minutes behind the railway, and saw no reason to change. An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one.

Nesting season arrives before the birds do, in the sense that the reeds seem to know it first. The last apple of the season always tasted, everyone agreed, a little better for being the last. A long friendship survives more silence than most people think it can.

My mother cut reeds the way her mother had, at the wrist and not the elbow, so the bed would recover by June. The workshop lamp burned oil at a rate its owner tracked more carefully than his own accounts. An old map, however wrong, still tells you what someone once believed to be true.

A heron stood so still at the tide line that I mistook it twice for a post before it proved me wrong. The harbor bell rang for fog more nights that year than anyone could remember from before. A garden planted in hope outlives, more often than not, the gardener's doubts about it.

The reed-cutter's daughter inherits calluses before she inherits opinions, which her mother considers the correct order. The evening chores went faster with two people than with one, though neither said so aloud. An old coat pocket, searched later, tells you where its owner had actually been.

Water in the channel runs brown after rain and clears again within a day, patient in a way I have never managed. The workshop's youngest apprentice asked more questions than the others combined, and was rarely told to stop. A river in flood forgives nothing and remembers everything, at least until the next flood.

We counted the nests each spring not from affection alone but because the count told us the season's temper. The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it. An unopened letter waits with a patience its writer rarely shared.

A basket of cut reed weighs more wet than it looks, a lesson every apprentice learns exactly once. The bakery's ovens stayed warm long after closing, heating the whole street a little further into the evening. A long-kept promise is worth more, if anything, for having been long-kept.

The marsh keeps its own calendar, indifferent to the one pinned above my mother's stove. The harbor emptied of boats by storm warning and filled again, cautiously, the following noon. An old friend recognized across a crowded market is a small, entirely disproportionate joy.

By June the reed bed stands taller than I do, and I have stopped minding being the smaller thing in the field. The workshop's ledgers, taken together, told a quieter story than either the profits or the losses alone. A garden wall built by hand outlasts, as a rule, the hands that built it.

A fox crossed the causeway at dusk with a bird in its mouth, unhurried, as though it had every right to it. Time moves at a different pace when there is work enough to fill it entirely. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect.

My mother taught me the difference between a reed worth cutting and one worth leaving, though she never explained why. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself.

The tide came in twice a day and asked nothing of us except that we remember to leave before it arrived. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it.

Nesting season ends the way most seasons end here, gradually, and then all at once in a single warm week. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright.

A reed-cutter's hands are read like a ledger by anyone who knows what they are looking at. A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company.

The marsh in April is the only season I have ever wanted to write down exactly as it happened. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved. A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both.

We sold the reed to the thatchers upriver, who complained about the price every year and paid it every year regardless. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential.

A heron's patience is the closest thing to a lesson the marsh ever offered me outright. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac.

My mother's calluses were, she said, the only inheritance she could guarantee would still be useful in fifty years. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was. A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own.

By the last cutting of the season the light goes long and gold across the water, and I have never once cut faster for it. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it. Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable.

The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count. A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference.

An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order.

The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness.

A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family. The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring. A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory.

The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close.

A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed.
